plan.chapter_thesis: Photonic AI accelerators demonstrate compelling throughput-per-watt for inference workloads that can be mapped to fixed or slowly varying linear transformations within scalable photonic computing systems, but training workloads requiring frequent weight updates, gradient computation, and mixed-precision arithmetic expose fundamental mismatches between photonic hardware capabilities and algorithmic requirements; co-design between AI algorithms and photonic computing hardware emerges as the critical enabler for closing this gap.
plan.reader_takeaway: While photonic computing offers unmatched energy efficiency for static inference tasks via all-optical matrix multiplication, its application to dynamic training is currently limited by hardware rigidity, necessitating a shift toward algorithm-hardware co-design and hybrid optoelectronic architectures rather than pure photonic replacement of electronic GPUs.

argument_sequence.purpose: Establish the core operational advantage of photonic systems for inference: high-throughput, low-latency linear transformations using inherent physical properties.
Quantify the performance benefits (throughput-per-watt) for specific inference classes while introducing the first major boundary: the difficulty of dynamic weight updates.
Detail the fundamental mismatch between photonic hardware staticity and the requirements of backpropagation-based training loops.
Introduce algorithm-hardware co-design as the primary strategy to bridge the precision and flexibility gap, focusing on inverse design methods.
Explain specific co-design techniques: using ML surrogates and physics-informed networks to optimize device structures for specific workloads.
Showcase successful implementations of co-designed, compact accelerators for fixed tasks (image classification) as proof-of-concept.
Address advanced architectural approaches (single-shot processing, heterogeneous integration) that attempt to scale beyond current limitations.
Synthesize the remaining gaps in benchmarking and system-level integration, framing them as open questions for future standardization.

terminology_rows.note: The joint optimization of neural network architectures and photonic device geometries to overcome hardware constraints like limited precision or static weights.
Using deep learning models to map desired optical responses to physical device structures, bypassing traditional iterative simulation.
Performing neural network forward passes entirely in the optical domain without intermediate electronic conversion.
A hybrid training strategy where optical neurons handle forward propagation while electronic/artificial neurons manage weight updates.

explanation_block_rows.title: The Physics of Photonic Inference
explanation_block_rows.goal: Define how photonic systems naturally implement linear algebra operations via superposition and interference, establishing the baseline advantage for inference.

explanation_block_rows.title: Performance Boundaries: Inference vs. Training
explanation_block_rows.goal: Contrast the high efficiency of static inference with the severe latency and flexibility bottlenecks encountered during dynamic training phases.

explanation_block_rows.title: Co-Design as the Critical Enabler
explanation_block_rows.goal: Introduce algorithm-hardware co-design and inverse design methodologies as the necessary response to hardware rigidity and precision limits.

explanation_block_rows.title: Advanced Inverse Design Strategies
explanation_block_rows.goal: Detail specific ML-driven techniques (surrogates, PINNs) that accelerate the discovery of optimal photonic structures for AI workloads.

explanation_block_rows.title: Demonstrated Accelerator Architectures
explanation_block_rows.goal: Present concrete examples of inverse-designed accelerators achieving compact, high-performance inference on standard benchmarks.

explanation_block_rows.title: Scaling Mechanisms and Integration
explanation_block_rows.goal: Discuss architectural innovations like single-shot processing and heterogeneous material integration that address scaling bottlenecks.

explanation_block_rows.title: Uncertainty and System-Level Gaps
explanation_block_rows.goal: Acknowledge limitations in current uncertainty quantification methods and the lack of standardized system-level benchmarks.

explanation_block_rows.title: Open Questions in Benchmarking and Integration
explanation_block_rows.goal: Explicitly state the missing evidence regarding end-to-end system benchmarks and the necessity of electronic-photonic memory integration.
